name: Drinking water frequently

lead: Drinking water frequently is a common suggestion in breath-care guides for dry mouth and mouth odour. The payoff people want is fresher breath, especially around the morning-breath window and long stretches of talking.

Water temporarily moistens the mouth and rinses away debris, though it does not restore saliva production. Wikipedia lists water among saliva substitutes without citing a specific trial, and notes breath is worst on waking because of overnight dryness.

paras: People keep a bottle at hand and sip regularly through the day, one guide suggesting every 15 to 30 minutes, with a glass by the bed or on waking. It is paired with brushing, tongue cleaning and other breath care.
It is a low-risk habit. A 2017 paper noted that bottled waters vary in pH. Breath that stays bad despite good hygiene and hydration is usually worth checking with a dentist or doctor.

angle.text: Frequent water sipping keeps the mouth moist, which reduces dry-mouth odour and leaves breath fresher. It is a low-cost habit common in breath-care guides; a 2019 Cochrane review found no strong evidence on which breath interventions work best.

lead: Drinking water frequently is a habit recommended in many dry-mouth and breath-care guides as a way to relieve a dry mouth and reduce mouth odour.[1][2] Wikipedia lists water among saliva substitutes but cites no specific trial for it.[3]

Grokipedia advises sipping water every 15 to 30 minutes, noting that large amounts at once give only temporary relief.[1] The Wikipedia halitosis article does not present water as a remedy, though it notes breath is worst on waking because of overnight dryness, and that a 2019 Cochrane review found no strong evidence on which interventions work best.[2]

paras: Saliva flow falls during sleep, and dehydration is a listed cause of dry mouth.[3] Intraoral halitosis is often located at the back of the tongue.[2]
No studies found. A 2017 paper examined pH levels in bottled water relevant to dry mouth.[4]
